claim: Sound encoding depends on the precise and reliable neurotransmission at the afferent synapses between the sensory inner hair cells (IHCs) and spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs).
source: Sound encoding depends on the precise and reliable neurotransmission at the afferent synapses between the sensory inner hair cells (IHCs) and spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about auditory system function.

claim: RTN4RL2 is expressed in SGNs and IHCs during cochlear development.
source: We observed Rtn4rl2 mRNA expression at E11.5 in the hair cell region and at E12.5 in both the spiral ganglion and hair cells (Figure 1B, C). Rtn4rl2 expression was further evident in hair cells at E16.5 and p1 (Figure 1D, E) and was maintained at low levels in spiral ganglia of p40 mice (Figure 1F).
evidence: RNAscope in situ hybridization data showing Rtn4rl2 mRNA at multiple developmental timepoints, visualized in Figure 1B-F.

claim: RTN4RL2 KO mice lack Rtn4rl2-specific mRNA puncta.
source: RTN4RL2 KO mice were lacking Rtn4rl2-specific mRNA puncta (Figure 1F), demonstrating specific detection of Rtn4rl2 expression in SGNs.
evidence: RNAscope ISH showing absence of Rtn4rl2 mRNA in RTN4RL2 KO mice compared to WT, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: SGN density is not changed in RTN4RL2 KO mice at p40.
source: We did not observe any change in SGN density or counts of inner and outer hair cells at p15, 1-month-, and 2-month-old mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of SGN density shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inner and outer hair cell counts are not affected in RTN4RL2 KO mice at p15, 1 month, and 2 months.
source: We did not observe any change in SGN density or counts of inner and outer hair cells at p15, 1-month-, and 2-month-old mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Hair cell counts shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The number of synaptic ribbons in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs is not changed at 3 weeks of age.
source: While we did not detect any change in the number of synaptic ribbons in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs, yet, ribbon volumes were bigger (Figure 2C, D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantification of Ctbp2-positive puncta shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ribbon volumes are enlarged in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs at 3 weeks of age.
source: While we did not detect any change in the number of synaptic ribbons in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs, yet, ribbon volumes were bigger (Figure 2C, D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantification of ribbon volumes shown in Figure 2D showing statistically significant increase (p < 0.001).

claim: Homer1 puncta juxtaposing IHC active zones are significantly smaller in RTN4RL2 KO mice compared to control IHCs.
source: Moreover, the Homer1 puncta juxtaposing IHC AZs were significantly smaller in RTN4RL2 KO mice compared to the control IHCs (Figure 2E).
evidence: Quantification of Homer1 patch volumes shown in Figure 2E with statistical significance (p < 0.001).

claim: The percentage of presynaptic ribbons juxtaposing Homer1 immunofluorescent puncta is decreased by approximately 7% in RTN4RL2 KO mice.
source: While we found the percentage of presynaptic ribbons juxtaposing Homer1 immunofluorescent puncta to be decreased by approximately 7% in RTN4RL2 KO mice (Figure 2F), we cannot exclude that our immunolabeling protocol lacked the sensitivity to detect smaller synaptically engaged PSDs.
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 2F with statistical significance (p = 0.03).

claim: Additional Homer1 patches appear away from IHCs in RTN4RL2 KO mice, potentially marking 'orphan' PSDs.
source: Interestingly, in addition to the Homer1-positive puncta juxtaposing presynaptic ribbons, we observed additional Homer1 patches, which appeared to be away from IHCs, potentially marking 'orphan' PSDs (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: Immunolabeling images in Figure 2A and B showing Homer1 puncta away from IHCs, marked with white arrowheads.

claim: Mature SGNs express GluA2–4 AMPA receptor subunits.
source: Out of the four pore-forming AMPA receptor subunits (GluA1–4), mature SGNs express GluA2–4 (Niedzielski and Wenthold, 1995; Matsubara et al., 1996).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Niedzielski and Wenthold, 1995; Matsubara et al., 1996).

claim: There is a severe reduction in the number of GluA2/3-positive puncta at RTN4RL2 KO IHCs.
source: Our immunolabeling of anti-GluA2/3 revealed a severe reduction in the number of GluA2/3-positive puncta at RTN4RL2 KO IHCs, indicating possible decrease or lack of GluA2/3 on the postsynaptic side of SGNs (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Immunolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 3A and B with statistical significance (p < 0.001).

claim: The remaining GluA2/3 patches do not properly juxtapose presynaptic ribbons in RTN4RL2 KO mice.
source: Interestingly, the remaining GluA2/3 patches did not properly juxtapose presynaptic ribbons (Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantification of colocalization shown in Figure 3C with statistical significance (p < 0.001).

claim: Gria2 mRNA expression is maintained in SGNs of RTN4RL2 KO mice.
source: Despite this, the expression of Gria2 mRNA appeared to be maintained in SGNs, as indicated by RNAscope (Figure 3D).
evidence: RNAscope ISH showing Gria2 mRNA expression in SGNs of both WT and KO mice, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GluA4 signal is not significantly detected at PSDs of RTN4RL2 KO SGNs compared to background.
source: Surprisingly, we did not detect a significant GluA4 signal compared to the background in RTN4RL2 KO cochleae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A substantial number of type I SGN neurites do not engage IHCs in RTN4RL2 KO organs of Corti (23 out of 83) compared to wild-type control (3 out of 32).
source: We observed a substantial number of neurites that did not engage the IHCs (non-synaptic neurites) in the RTN4RL2 KO organs of Corti (23 out of 83) in contrast to the wild-type control (3 out of 32, Figure 4E).
evidence: SBEM reconstruction data quantified in Figure 4E showing statistical significance (p = 0.032).

claim: Most non-synaptic neurites in RTN4RL2 KO mice are found in the inner spiral bundle but fail to reach IHC basal lateral poles (17 out of 23).
source: Although most non-synaptic neurites were found in the inner spiral bundle, they failed to reach IHC basal lateral poles to form contacts (17 out of 23 in RTN4RL2 KO animals).
evidence: SBEM reconstruction analysis of neurite trajectories.

claim: Nearly all traced radial fibers are predominantly unbranched in both RTN4RL2 KO (97%) and wild-type control mice (94%).
source: Nevertheless, nearly all traced radial fibers were found predominantly unbranched in both the RTN4RL2 KO (97%) and the wild-type control mice (94%; Figure 4F).
evidence: SBEM reconstruction data quantified in Figure 4F (p = 0.226, not significant).

claim: The presence of non-synaptic neurites in RTN4RL2 KO animals is not associated with a profound reduction in ribbon synapses.
source: Note that the presence of non-synaptic neurites in the RTN4RL2 KO animals was not associated with a profound reduction in ribbon synapses (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a different scenario than deafferentation due to excitotoxic synaptopathy as recently reported (Moverman et al., 2023).
evidence: Comparison of ribbon synapse counts across multiple figures with citation to Moverman et al., 2023.

claim: Maximal Ca2+ current amplitude is not changed in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs.
source: We did not observe any change in the maximal Ca2+ current amplitude (Figure 5B, C), yet noticed small (∼+3 mV) but consistent and statistically significant depolarized shift of the voltage of half-maximal Ca2+ channel activation (Vhalf; Figure 5D, E).
evidence: Patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5B and C (p = 0.47, not significant).

claim: There is a small (~+3 mV) but statistically significant depolarized shift of the voltage of half-maximal Ca2+ channel activation in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs.
source: We did not observe any change in the maximal Ca2+ current amplitude (Figure 5B, C), yet noticed small (∼+3 mV) but consistent and statistically significant depolarized shift of the voltage of half-maximal Ca2+ channel activation (Vhalf; Figure 5D, E).
evidence: Patch-clamp recordings and Boltzmann fit analysis shown in Figure 5D and E (p = 0.004).

claim: The voltage sensitivity of Ca2+ channels is not changed in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs.
source: The voltage sensitivity of the channels was not changed in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs (Figure 5F).
evidence: Patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5F (p = 0.93, not significant).

claim: Both fast and sustained components of exocytosis remain intact in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs.
source: Both fast (up to 20 ms depolarization) and sustained components of exocytosis remained intact in the mutant, indicating unaffected readily releasable pool and replenishment of the vesicles in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs (Figure 5H).
evidence: Perforated patch-clamp capacitance measurements shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Maximal Ca2+ influx at single active zones tends to be higher in IHCs of RTN4RL2 KO mice, but the difference does not reach statistical significance.
source: Maximal Ca2+ influx at single AZs tended to be higher in IHCs of RTN4RL2 KO mice, but the difference did not reach statistical significance (Figure 6B, Bi).
evidence: Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 6B and Bi (p = 0.24, not significant).

claim: The Vhalf of Ca2+ channel clusters at single active zones shows a depolarized shift (~+5 mV) in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs.
source: The Vhalf of Ca2+ channel clusters at single AZs showed depolarized shift (∼+5 mV), which was statistically significant despite the large variability of Vhalf across different AZs (Figure 6C, Ci).
evidence: Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 6C and Ci (p = 0.002).

claim: There is no mismatch between Ctbp2-positive puncta and evoked Ca2+ hotspots in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs.
source: Furthermore, we did not observe any mismatch in Ctbp2-positive puncta and evoked Ca2+ hotspots, indicating the correct localization of Ca2+ channels at the AZs.
evidence: Ca2+ imaging analysis comparing Ctbp2 and Ca2+ hotspot locations.

claim: CaV1.3, Ctbp2, and Bassoon protein clusters do not show apparent misalignment in RTN4RL2 KO IHCs.
source: We verified this by performing immunostainings of CaV1.3, Ctbp2, and Bassoon and did not detect any apparent misalignment of these protein clusters (Figure 6D).
evidence: Immunolabeling shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ABR thresholds are significantly increased by around 30–45 dB across all tested frequencies and in response to click stimulations in RTN4RL2 KO mice compared to wild-type controls.
source: We found ABR thresholds to be significantly increased by around 30–45 dB across all the tested frequencies and in response to the click stimulations in RTN4RL2 KO mice compared to the wild-type controls (Figure 7).
evidence: ABR measurements shown in Figure 7 with statistical significance.

claim: RTN4RL2 heterozygous mice show an intermediate phenotype with ABR threshold increases of approximately 10–15 dB at 4, 16, and 32 kHz frequencies.
source: RTN4RL2 heterozygous (RTN4RL2 HET) mice showed an intermediate phenotype between the RTN4RL2 KO and RTN4RL2 WT mice with a lower yet significant increase of ABR thresholds of approximately 10–15 dB at 4, 16, and 32 kHz frequencies.
evidence: ABR measurements shown in Figure 7.

claim: RTN4RL2 is required for normal hearing.
source: Finally, ABR thresholds were elevated in RTN4RL2 KO mice, indicating that RTN4RL2 is required for normal hearing.
evidence: ABR data showing elevated thresholds in RTN4RL2 KO mice.

claim: RTN4RL2 contributes to the proper formation and function of auditory afferent synapses.
source: Together, these findings suggest that RTN4RL2 contributes to the proper formation and function of auditory afferent synapses and is critical for normal hearing.
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental findings including synaptic alterations and hearing impairment.

claim: RTN4 receptors have been implicated as presynaptic adhesion molecules based on their transsynaptic interactions with postsynaptically enriched BAI adhesion GPCRs.
source: RTN4 receptors have been implicated as presynaptic adhesion molecules based on their transsynaptic interactions with postsynaptically enriched brain-specific angiogenesis inhibitor (BAI) adhesion GPCRs (Stephenson et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Stephenson et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021).

claim: RTN4R has been proposed to function postsynaptically, given that its knockdown leads primarily to postsynaptic changes.
source: Despite this, at least RTN4R has been proposed to function postsynaptically, given that its knockdown leads primarily to postsynaptic changes (Wills et al., 2012).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Wills et al., 2012).

claim: BAI1-deficient mice show hearing impairment and absence or decrease of different AMPA receptor subunits at SGN postsynapses.
source: Interestingly, a recent study described a hearing impairment in BAI1-deficient mice and suggested that postsynaptically functioning BAI1 is important for correct localization of AMPA receptor subunits in SGNs based on the absence or decrease of different AMPA receptor subunits at the SGN postsynapses in BAI1-deficient mice (Carlton et al., 2024).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Carlton et al., 2024).

claim: The GluA2–4 AMPA receptor subunit localization to SGN PSDs may require the interaction of presynaptic RTN4RL2 and postsynaptic BAI1.
source: Along with the evidence for transsynaptic interaction between RTN4Rs and BAIs (Wang et al., 2021), this raises the possibility that the GluA2–4 AMPA receptor subunit localization to SGN PSDs requires the interaction of presynaptic RTN4RL2 and postsynaptic BAI1.
evidence: Inference based on similarity between RTN4RL2 KO and BAI1 KO phenotypes, combined with known RTN4R-BAI interactions.

claim: Presynaptic changes in IHCs can result from postsynaptic manipulation in SGNs.
source: Presynaptic changes upon postsynaptic manipulation have been reported previously. For instance, the deletion of postsynaptically expressed Pou4f1 transcription factor resulted in hyperpolarized shift of IHC Ca2+ channels, as well as in changes of the presynaptic heterogeneity of IHC AZs (Sherrill et al., 2019). Similarly, presynaptic ribbon sizes were altered in IHCs of mice, which exhibited conditional deletion of Runx1 transcription factor from SGNs (Shrestha et al., 2023).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Sherrill et al., 2019; Shrestha et al., 2023).

claim: The afferent synaptic changes contribute to the severe hearing impairment in RTN4RL2 KO mice.
source: We propose that the afferent synaptic changes contribute to the severe hearing impairment in RTN4RL2 KO mice.
evidence: Inference based on observed synaptic alterations and hearing phenotype.

claim: The apparent Ca2+ dependence of glutamate release from IHCs on average follows a near linear relationship.
source: As it has been shown, the apparent Ca2+ dependence of glutamate release from IHCs on average follows a near linear relationship (Wong et al., 2014; Özçete and Moser, 2021; Jaime Tobón and Moser, 2023a; Jaime Tobón and Moser, 2023b).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Wong et al., 2014; Özçete and Moser, 2021; Jaime Tobón and Moser, 2023a; Jaime Tobón and Moser, 2023b).

claim: Due to the depolarized shift of Ca2+ channel activation, glutamate release from IHCs would require stronger stimuli in RTN4RL2 KO mice.
source: Therefore, due to the depolarized shift of the Ca2+ channel activation, the glutamate release from IHCs would require stronger stimuli.
evidence: Logical inference based on the observed depolarized shift and known Ca2+-release relationship.

claim: Depolarized activation of Ca2+ channels in Ribeye knock-out mice is associated with higher firing thresholds and lower spontaneous rates in SGNs.
source: This could result in increased sound thresholds, as shown in Ribeye knock-out mice, where depolarized activation of Ca2+ channels has been associated with higher firing thresholds and lower spontaneous rates in SGNs, although a less severe hearing phenotype was observed in those mice (Jean et al., 2018).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Jean et al., 2018).

claim: Direct manipulation of the voltage dependence of Cav1.3 Ca2+ channel activation results in changes of SGN firing and potentially auditory thresholds.
source: Furthermore, we have shown recently that a direct manipulation of the voltage dependence of Cav1.3 Ca2+ channel activation results in changes of SGN firing and potentially auditory thresholds, further supporting our hypothesis of sound threshold elevation in RTN4RL2 KO mice being caused by the depolarized activation of Ca2+ channels in IHCs (Karagulyan et al., 2025).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Karagulyan et al., 2025).

claim: GluA3 KO mice display reduced GluA2 signal at SGN PSDs but intact auditory thresholds.
source: Compared to GluA3 KO mice, which display reduced GluA2 signal at SGN PSDs but intact auditory thresholds, the increased auditory thresholds in RTN4RL2 KO mice could additionally be caused by the lack of GluA4 subunits juxtaposing presynaptic ribbons, which, in contrast, were shown to be upregulated in GluA3 KO mice (Rutherford et al., 2023).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Rutherford et al., 2023).

claim: GluA4 subunits are upregulated in GluA3 KO mice.
source: Compared to GluA3 KO mice, which display reduced GluA2 signal at SGN PSDs but intact auditory thresholds, the increased auditory thresholds in RTN4RL2 KO mice could additionally be caused by the lack of GluA4 subunits juxtaposing presynaptic ribbons, which, in contrast, were shown to be upregulated in GluA3 KO mice (Rutherford et al., 2023).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Rutherford et al., 2023).

claim: The 'orphan' PSDs observed around IHCs in RTN4RL2 KO mice are not part of efferent synapses formed between LOC/MOCs and SGNs.
source: These 'orphan' PSDs seem not to be part of the efferent synapses formed between LOC/MOCs and SGNs as we verified by simultaneous anti-Homer1 and anti-synapsin immunolabelings.
evidence: Immunolabeling data showing lack of juxtaposition between Homer1 and synapsin puncta.

claim: SGN neurite retraction from IHCs has been demonstrated in noise-exposed animals, followed by degeneration of SGN somata and axons.
source: SGN neurite retraction from IHCs has been demonstrated in noise-exposed animals, followed by the degeneration of the SGN somata and axons (Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Kujawa and Liberman, 2015; Moverman et al., 2023).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Kujawa and Liberman, 2015; Moverman et al., 2023).

claim: Noise-induced SGN neurite retraction results in up to 50% degeneration of ribbon synapses.
source: This process, however, results in up to 50% degeneration of the ribbon synapses.
evidence: Referenced from literature on noise-induced synaptopathy.

claim: The non-synaptic neurites in RTN4RL2 KO mice do not result from synaptic loss as found in hereditary or acquired synaptopathy.
source: This indicates that the non-synaptic neurites do not result from synaptic loss as found in hereditary or acquired synaptopathy (Roux et al., 2006; Ruel et al., 2008; Seal et al., 2008; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009).
evidence: Inference based on maintained ribbon synapse and SGN counts, with citations to synaptopathy literature (Roux et al., 2006; Ruel et al., 2008; Seal et al., 2008; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009).

claim: Major synaptic pruning takes place in developing SGNs, whereby up to 50% of synapses are lost between IHCs and SGNs.
source: Alternatively, it is known that major synaptic pruning takes place in developing SGNs, whereby up to 50% of the synapses are lost between the IHCs and the SGNs (Defourny et al., 2013; Coate et al., 2019), suggesting that the non-synaptic SGN neurites of RTN4RL2 KO mice could be a result of failed pruning of SGNs during the development.
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Defourny et al., 2013; Coate et al., 2019).

claim: The non-synaptic SGN neurites of RTN4RL2 KO mice could be a result of failed pruning of SGNs during development.
source: Alternatively, it is known that major synaptic pruning takes place in developing SGNs, whereby up to 50% of the synapses are lost between the IHCs and the SGNs (Defourny et al., 2013; Coate et al., 2019), suggesting that the non-synaptic SGN neurites of RTN4RL2 KO mice could be a result of failed pruning of SGNs during the development.
evidence: Speculation based on known developmental pruning processes and observed phenotype.

claim: The only well-established ligand for RTN4RL2 is MAG.
source: While RTN4R in-trans interactions include NogoA, MAG, OMgp, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, the only well-established ligand for RTN4RL2 remains MAG (Fournier et al., 2001; Domeniconi et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002b; Venkatesh et al., 2005; Schwab, 2010).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Fournier et al., 2001; Domeniconi et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002b; Venkatesh et al., 2005; Schwab, 2010).

claim: BAI–RTN4R interaction has been suggested to mediate dendritic arborization, axonal elongation, and synapse formation in iPSC-derived neurons.
source: BAI–RTN4R interaction has been suggested to mediate dendritic arborization, axonal elongation, synapse formation in iPSC-derived neurons (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Wang et al., 2021).

claim: RTN4RL2 has been proposed to interact with chondroitin-sulfate proteoglycan versican to control the amount of skin innervation by DRG neurites.
source: Finally, RTN4RL2 has been proposed to interact with chondroitin-sulfate proteoglycan versican to control the amount of skin innervation by DRG neurites (Bäumer et al., 2014).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Bäumer et al., 2014).

claim: Extracellular matrix proteins such as aggrecan, brevican, Tenascin-R, Tenascin-C, hyaluron, and proteoglycan link proteins 1 and 4 form dense, basket-like structures that surround the base of IHCs.
source: While to our knowledge, attempts have yet to be made for detecting versican signal around the IHCs, other extracellular matrix proteins such as aggrecan, brevican, Tenascin-R, Tenascin-C, hyaluron, and proteoglycan link proteins 1 and 4 have been shown to form dense, basket-like structures that surround the base of the IHCs (Kwiatkowska et al., 2016; Sonntag et al., 2018).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Kwiatkowska et al., 2016; Sonntag et al., 2018).

claim: Deletion of brevican results in alteration of pre- and postsynaptic spatial coupling at IHC synapses.
source: Furthermore, deletion of brevican results in alteration of pre- and postsynaptic spatial coupling at IHC synapses, indicating the possible role of extracellular matrix in transsynaptic organization.
evidence: Referenced from literature on brevican function in the cochlea.

claim: SGN neurites extend and reach IHCs at late embryonic stages (E16.5) in mice.
source: In mice, SGN neurites extend and reach IHCs at late embryonic stages (E16.5; Koundakjian et al., 2007), whereby early synaptic contacts are established between the two cells at E18 (Michanski et al., 2019).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Koundakjian et al., 2007; Michanski et al., 2019).

claim: Early synaptic contacts are established between IHCs and SGNs at E18 in mice.
source: In mice, SGN neurites extend and reach IHCs at late embryonic stages (E16.5; Koundakjian et al., 2007), whereby early synaptic contacts are established between the two cells at E18 (Michanski et al., 2019).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Michanski et al., 2019).

claim: Developmental changes and maturation of afferent synapses continue until the onset of hearing (p12), with further refinement occurring till the fourth postnatal week.
source: Developmental changes and maturation of afferent synapses continue until the onset of hearing (p12), with further refinement occurring till the fourth postnatal week (Wong et al., 2014; Liberman and Liberman, 2016; Michanski et al., 2019).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Wong et al., 2014; Liberman and Liberman, 2016; Michanski et al., 2019).

claim: In mature cochleae, each IHC receives contact from 5 to 30 SGNs.
source: In mature cochleae, each IHC receives a contact from 5 to 30 SGNs, while each SGN contacts only one active zone (AZ) of one IHC in the majority of cases (Meyer and Moser, 2010; Hua et al., 2021).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Meyer and Moser, 2010; Hua et al., 2021).

claim: Each SGN contacts only one active zone of one IHC in the majority of cases in mature cochleae.
source: In mature cochleae, each IHC receives a contact from 5 to 30 SGNs, while each SGN contacts only one active zone (AZ) of one IHC in the majority of cases (Meyer and Moser, 2010; Hua et al., 2021).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Meyer and Moser, 2010; Hua et al., 2021).

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been implicated in SGN neurite guidance and establishment of IHC innervation by SGNs, including signaling via EphrinA5–EphA4, Neuropilin2/Semaphorin3F, Semaphorin5B/PlexinA1, and Semaphorin3A.
source: To this date, multiple mechanisms have been implicated in SGN neurite guidance and establishment of IHC innervation by SGNs, including signaling via EphrinA5–EphA4, Neuropilin2/Semaphorin3F, Semaphorin5B/PlexinA1, and Semaphorin3A (Defourny et al., 2013; Coate et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2019; Cantu-Guerra et al., 2023).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Defourny et al., 2013; Coate et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2019; Cantu-Guerra et al., 2023).

claim: Synaptic adhesion proteins such as neurexins and neuroligins have been suggested to play a role in pre- and postsynaptic assemblies at IHC afferent synapses.
source: Similar to the central conventional synapses, synaptic adhesion proteins such as neurexins and neuroligins have been suggested to play a role in pre- and postsynaptic assemblies (Ramirez et al., 2022; Jukic et al., 2024).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Ramirez et al., 2022; Jukic et al., 2024).

claim: The CaV1.3 extracellular auxiliary subunit CaVα2δ2 is important for proper alignment of presynaptic IHC AZs and postsynaptic densities of SGNs.
source: Furthermore, the CaV1.3 extracellular auxiliary subunit CaVα2δ2 was indicated to be important for proper alignment of presynaptic IHC AZs and postsynaptic densities (PSDs) of SGNs (Fell et al., 2016).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Fell et al., 2016).

claim: RTN4Rs are leucine-rich repeat (LRR) and glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchored cell surface receptors.
source: RTN4Rs are leucine-rich repeat (LRR) and glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchored cell surface receptors (Figure 1A).
evidence: Structural description shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The primary role of RTN4Rs is thought to limit synaptic plasticity and axonal outgrowth as well as to restrict axonal regeneration after injury.
source: Their primary role is thought to limit synaptic plasticity and axonal outgrowth as well as to restrict axonal regeneration after injury (reviewed in Mironova and Giger, 2013).
evidence: Referenced from review (Mironova and Giger, 2013).

claim: RTN4R and RTN4RL1 are involved in axonal guidance.
source: While RTN4R and RTN4RL1 are involved in axonal guidance (Vaccaro et al., 2022), RTN4RL2 has been proposed to be important for innervation of the epidermis by dorsal root ganglion neurons (Bäumer et al., 2014).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Vaccaro et al., 2022).

claim: RTN4RL2 has been proposed to be important for innervation of the epidermis by dorsal root ganglion neurons.
source: While RTN4R and RTN4RL1 are involved in axonal guidance (Vaccaro et al., 2022), RTN4RL2 has been proposed to be important for innervation of the epidermis by dorsal root ganglion neurons (Bäumer et al., 2014).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Bäumer et al., 2014).

claim: RTN4Rs are suggested to control the number and development of synapses.
source: Furthermore, RTN4Rs are suggested to control the number and the development of synapses (Wills et al., 2012) and to play a role in transsynaptic signaling (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Wills et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2021).

claim: RTN4Rs play a role in transsynaptic signaling.
source: Furthermore, RTN4Rs are suggested to control the number and the development of synapses (Wills et al., 2012) and to play a role in transsynaptic signaling (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Wang et al., 2021).

claim: Recent single-cell transcriptomic studies of the cochlea detected the expression of RTN4Rs in SGNs and IHCs.
source: Recent single-cell transcriptomic studies of the cochlea detected the expression of RTN4Rs in SGNs and IHCs (Shrestha et al., 2018; Jean et al., 2023).
evidence: Referenced from published literature (Shrestha et al., 2018; Jean et al., 2023).
